title: Engineering & Incident Cases
sub: Outages, slow systems, trade-offs and technical decisions under pressure.

cards.scenario: Your API's response time jumped from 200 ms to 2 seconds right after a deployment.
cards.question: What are your first steps?
answer: Roll back first if users are affected, then investigate
Compare the deploy diff: new queries, removed indexes, added calls
Check database, cache hit rate and downstream service latency
Add a latency alert and a load test for that path to prevent a repeat

cards.scenario: A nightly batch job that used to take 1 hour now takes 6 hours, and data grew only 20%.
cards.question: How would you investigate?
answer: Profile the job to find which step got slower
Look for queries that switched to full table scans
Check for lock contention with other jobs running at night
Fix the hot spot, then add runtime monitoring with an alert

cards.scenario: Customers report being charged twice for one order, about 1 in 1,000 orders.
cards.question: How would you find and fix the problem?
answer: Refund affected customers and confirm the scope from payment records
Look for client or network retries that resend the payment request
Add idempotency keys so repeated requests charge only once
Add a daily reconciliation check between orders and payments

cards.scenario: Your team must choose between building a feature in-house or buying a vendor tool.
cards.question: How would you decide?
answer: Ask whether it is core to your product or a commodity
Compare total cost: build and maintain vs licence and integrate
Consider time to market, vendor lock-in and data security
Run a short proof of concept before committing

cards.scenario: A flash sale is expected to bring 10 times normal traffic next week.
cards.question: How would you prepare the system?
answer: Load test the critical path: browse, cart and checkout
Scale ahead of time and add caching for product pages
Add rate limits, a queue and graceful fallbacks for non-critical features
Prepare dashboards, an on-call rota and a rollback plan

cards.scenario: Tests in your CI pipeline fail randomly about 10% of the time, and developers ignore failures.
cards.question: What would you do?
answer: Measure: track which tests fail without code changes
Quarantine the flakiest tests so the pipeline is trusted again
Fix common causes: timing, shared state, test order, network calls
Make a flaky-test budget and an owner part of the team's process

cards.scenario: A database is close to its storage limit and will be full in about three weeks.
cards.question: How would you handle it?
answer: Buy time immediately: increase storage or archive old data
Find what grows fastest — logs, audit tables, soft-deleted rows
Set retention policies and move cold data to cheaper storage
Add capacity alerts well before the limit next time

cards.scenario: Your team has a lot of technical debt and the product manager only wants new features.
cards.question: How would you make the case for fixing it?
answer: Show the cost in business terms: slower delivery, incidents, bugs
Pick the debt that blocks upcoming features first
Propose a steady share, e.g. 20% of each sprint
Measure and report the improvement in speed and stability

cards.scenario: A security researcher reports that user emails can be seen through a public API.
cards.question: What are your next steps?
answer: Confirm the issue and close the leak as fast as possible
Check logs to see whether it was exploited and which data was exposed
Inform security, legal and affected users as required
Hold a post-mortem and add access checks and tests for the API

cards.scenario: Mobile app crashes rose from 0.5% to 3% of sessions after a new release.
cards.question: How would you respond?
answer: Pause the staged rollout to stop the spread
Group crash reports by stack trace, device and OS version
Ship a hotfix or turn off the feature with a flag
Add the failing case to tests and release checks
